# Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns

**Section and topic:** Section 1 - Conditional variance models (ARCH and GARCH).

**Type of project:** Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. The GARCH(1,1) likelihood is coded from first principles.

**Aim:** To model and forecast the volatility of daily JSE All Share Index (ALSI) returns, and to determine which model, ARCH, GARCH or GJR-GARCH, gives the best out-of-sample volatility forecasts compared to the constant-variance and EWMA benchmarks.

**Data used:**

-   Daily FTSE/JSE All Share total return index (J203, dividends reinvested), 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. Source: Gebbie, T. (2020), *Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994--2017*, University of Cape Town, <https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1>.

Daily log returns (%) were modelled. July 1995 to December 2012 is used as the training set and January 2013 to February 2017 as the test set. Download instructions are in the detailed analysis.

**Methods used:** The mean equation is selected by comparing candidate ARIMA models using BIC. The residuals of this model are tested for ARCH effects using the Ljung-Box test on the squared residuals and Engle's ARCH LM test. The order of a pure ARCH model is chosen using BIC and compared to a GARCH($1,1$) model with the same mean and normal innovations. The candidate models, ARCH($q$), GARCH($1,1$) with normal and Student-$t$ innovations and GJR-GARCH($1,1$) with Student-$t$ innovations, are estimated by maximum likelihood. The GARCH($1,1$) likelihood is coded from first principles and maximised using `optim`. The fitted models are assessed using diagnostics on the standardised residuals. The rolling one-day ahead volatility forecasts are compared to the constant-variance and EWMA benchmarks using MSE and QLIKE, Diebold--Mariano tests of equal predictive accuracy and Value-at-Risk backtests. The optimal model is used to forecast volatility over the following 63 trading days.

**Key findings:**

-   The returns are only weakly autocorrelated, so an AR(1) mean model is sufficient. However, there is strong evidence of ARCH effects ($p$ \< 0.001). Thus, volatility is predictable even though returns are not.
-   A pure ARCH model requires 11 lags and still has a higher BIC than a GARCH(1,1) model. Volatility shocks in the ARCH model have a half-life \< 5 trading days as opposed to the GARCH models with half-lives ranging from 55 to 98 trading days.
-   GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student-$t$ errors is the best model both in sample (BIC = 2.983) and out of sample (QLIKE = 0.805), outperforming EWMA (QLIKE = 0.849) and the constant-variance model (QLIKE = 1.063). Negative shocks increase the following day's variance approximately 2.8 times more than positive shocks of the same size. Volatility is highly persistent (persistence = 0.987) and the errors have heavier tails than the normal distribution ($\hat{\nu} = 9.9$).
-   Diebold--Mariano tests show that at the 5% level, GJR-GARCH-$t$ has a significantly lower QLIKE loss than Constant, EWMA, ARCH, GARCH-N, and GARCH-t. 
-   Value-at-Risk backtests show that at the 1% level, Constant, GARCH-t, and GJR-GARCH-t pass both tests, while EWMA, ARCH, and GARCH-N are rejected by at least one test.
-   My implementation of the GARCH(1,1) likelihood, from first principles, reproduced the `rugarch` estimates to 3 decimal places.
-   At the end of the sample, volatility (13.0% p.a.) is below its long-run level (19.0% p.a.). Thus, the forecast rises slowly towards the long-run level and reaches 16.8% p.a. after 63 trading days.

**What I would do differently next time:**

-   The returns are negatively skewed, which a symmetric Student-$t$ distribution cannot capture. I would compare the models with skewed Student-$t$ innovations.
-   I would extend the dataset beyond February 2017. This would allow for current volatility forecasts and would test the stability of the estimated parameters.
